🏠 Internal / LAN Scanner

Scan a host or subnet on your private network. In-browser discovery finds reachable services, while the TLS Inspect action can inspect a TLS service on any discovered TCP port (for example 4443, 8443 or 10443). Certificate and lower-protocol enumeration on private/custom TLS ports requires the optional internal helper because browsers cannot expose raw TLS peer certificates.

TCP Connect Scan Subnet Host Discovery Internal DNS HTTP Fingerprint TLS & nmap
⚪ Browser-only scan (no install required)
🧰 Browser-only discovery: the internal scanner can find reachable services without installation. Use TLS Inspect on any discovered TCP port for real certificate details and enabled-version enumeration when the optional internal helper is available.
Accepts https:// / http:// URLs, host:port, bare IPs, subnets (CIDR) and hostnames. For a custom TLS listener, enter a current DHCP address or stable hostname, e.g. https://device.local:9443, then select Inspect TLS Port.
💡 Dynamic IP / DHCP: use a stable hostname or mDNS name (for example device.local), or scan the current subnet/CIDR and click TLS Inspect beside the discovered service. The discovered host address is passed dynamically—no fixed address is used.
🔢 Full TCP range 1–65535 All ports scanned; classified OPEN / CLOSED / FILTERED. For DHCP/dynamic hosts, scan a CIDR or use a hostname, then inspect the discovered service.
🧰 No server needed: the internal scanner does a full 1–65535 sweep directly in the browser with no server and no installation. The ⚙️ Setup button (above) is only for the optional Control Daemon if you want the Node helper for more authoritative real TCP connect results (nothing is installed — run it only when needed).

📚 Content Security Policy (CSP) Directives Reference Guide Expand Guide & Source Values ▾

Content Security Policy (CSP) directives control what resources (scripts, styles, images) a browser can load and execute on a webpage. They are sent via the Content-Security-Policy HTTP header to mitigate XSS attacks and unauthorized data exfiltration.

1. Fetch Directives (Resource Loading)
  • default-src: Serves as the fallback for all other fetch directives when unspecified.
  • script-src: Restricts allowed sources for JavaScript. (Variants: script-src-elem for <script> tags, script-src-attr for inline event handlers)
  • style-src: Restricts allowed sources for CSS stylesheets. (Variants: style-src-elem, style-src-attr)
  • img-src: Restricts sources for images and favicons.
  • connect-src: Restricts endpoints for fetch(), XMLHttpRequest, WebSockets, and EventSource.
  • font-src: Restricts allowed web fonts loaded via @font-face.
  • frame-src: Controls valid URLs for nested frames (<iframe>, <frame>).
  • media-src: Restricts sources for audio and video (<audio>, <video>).
  • object-src: Restricts sources for plugins (<object>, <embed>).
  • worker-src: Controls sources for Web Workers, Shared Workers, and Service Workers.
  • manifest-src: Controls application manifest files.
2. Document & Navigation Directives
  • base-uri: Restricts URLs allowed in a document's <base> element.
  • form-action: Controls valid target URLs for HTML form submissions.
  • frame-ancestors: Specifies which domains can embed current page inside <iframe> / <frame> (prevents Clickjacking).
  • sandbox: Enables standard iframe-style restrictions (e.g. blocking popups or scripts unless allowed).
3. Reporting & Enforcement Directives
  • report-uri / report-to: Specifies endpoints where browser sends JSON report payloads when violations occur.
  • upgrade-insecure-requests: Instructs browsers to automatically rewrite HTTP requests to HTTPS before loading.
  • require-trusted-types-for: Forces DOM-based XSS protections requiring Trusted Types for dangerous sinks like innerHTML.
4. Common Source Values
  • 'self': Allows resources from exact same origin (same scheme, host, and port).
  • 'none': Completely blocks loading that resource type.
  • 'unsafe-inline': Permits inline scripts/styles (increases XSS risk).
  • 'unsafe-eval': Allows string-to-code execution APIs like eval().
  • 'nonce-<base64>': Permits inline scripts/styles matching a cryptographically generated token.

SSL certificate & TLS configuration

Not analyzed

This section verifies the certificate actually deployed by the target and, for standard HTTPS port 443, runs a Qualys SSL Labs deep assessment to enumerate SSLv2/SSLv3, TLS 1.0/1.1/1.2/1.3, cipher suites and known TLS weaknesses. The certificate card shows subject, issuer, Not Before, UTC Not After/expiry date, serial number, SHA-256 fingerprint, SANs and chain. SSL Labs results include deprecated protocol versions and reported vulnerabilities such as POODLE, Heartbleed, BEAST, FREAK, Logjam, DROWN, CRIME/TLS compression and ROBOT/Bleichenbacher. Certificate Transparency records are not used as a substitute for the deployed certificate.
